subject: physics
question_text: Explain the working of a hydraulic lift and hydraulic brakes.

mark_split.label: The master cylinder feeds four wheel cylinders

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 10 (Mechanical Properties of Fluids), Short Answer Question 4 (printed p.108). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The four-way mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: both devices work by Pascal's law; in the hydraulic lift a force F₁ on a small piston of area A₁ gives pressure P = F₁/A₁, and the same pressure acting on the large piston of area A₂ gives F₂ = F₁ × A₂/A₁; in hydraulic brakes the force on the brake pedal produces a pressure that is transmitted through the brake fluid to the cylinders at all four wheels equally and at the same instant. This card explains how the two named devices work; a separate question states Pascal's law itself and names the applications, including the hydraulic press.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Both use Pascal's law
steps.margin_note: First mark. Name Pascal's law before describing either device.
steps.why: Both mechanisms are the same law used two different ways, so stating the shared law first is what makes the rest of the answer read as one explanation.
common_mistakes: Describing the lift and the brakes without ever naming the law both rest on.
Stating the law for liquids only, when Pascal's law holds for any fluid at rest.

recall.must_convey: That both the lift and the brakes work by Pascal's law, pressure applied to an enclosed fluid transmitted undiminished.
accept: both devices use the same law
reject: F2 equals F1 into A2 by A1

steps.memory_tip: One law, two machines: the lift and the brakes both transmit pressure undiminished.

steps.label: The hydraulic lift

piston of area A₁ gives a
Since A₂ is much larger than

steps.margin_note: Second mark. Set up the pressure equality, then the force multiplication F₂ = F₁ × (A₂/A₁).
steps.why: The pressure set at the small piston is the same at the large piston, since the fluid is enclosed and connects them; the same pressure acting over a much larger area multiplies the force, with no extra force supplied by hand.
common_mistakes: Mixing up which piston is A₁, small, force applied, and which is A₂, large, load carried.
Saying the force is multiplied by A₁/A₂ instead of A₂/A₁ — that would make F₂ smaller.

recall.must_convey: That F1 on the small piston A1 gives a pressure P equal to F1 by A1, the same pressure acts on the large piston, and F2 equals F1 times A2 over A1, so a small force lifts a much larger load.
accept: P equals F1 by A1 equals F2 by A2
F2 equals F1 into A2 by A1
reject: brake fluid to all four wheels

steps.memory_tip: F₂ = F₁ × (A₂/A₁) — the bigger the second piston, the bigger the lift.

steps.label: The master cylinder feeds four wheel cylinders
steps.mark_note: One master cylinder, four wheel cylinders
lines: the brake fluid, which fills a
cylinder at each of the four
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Name the master cylinder and say it feeds all four wheel cylinders through the brake fluid.
steps.why: One master cylinder pushing on the enclosed brake fluid is what lets a single pedal press reach every wheel, instead of needing a separate pedal for each one.
common_mistakes: Describing only one wheel's cylinder and not saying the same master cylinder feeds all four.
Leaving out the master cylinder and saying the pedal itself presses the brake fluid.

recall.must_convey: That pressing the pedal moves a piston in the master cylinder, which pushes brake fluid through pipes to a wheel cylinder at each of the four wheels.
accept: master cylinder pushes the brake fluid
one master cylinder feeds four wheel cylinders
pipes connect the master cylinder to each wheel
reject: F2 equals F1 into A2 by A1

steps.memory_tip: One master cylinder, one push, four wheel cylinders fed by the same fluid.

steps.label: Equal, simultaneous braking
steps.mark_note: Same braking at every wheel, same instant
lines: set at the master cylinder is
A_master is the area of the
every wheel is braked by the
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Say that every wheel gets the same pressure at the same instant, and name A_master.
steps.why: The same pressure reaches every wheel cylinder at the same instant, so identical wheel cylinders produce the same braking force.
common_mistakes: Describing only one wheel's cylinder and not saying the same pressure reaches all four.
Saying the four wheels brake one after another instead of at the same instant.

recall.must_convey: That the pressure set at the master cylinder is transmitted undiminished to all four wheel cylinders at the same instant, so identical wheel cylinders give the same braking force.
accept: same pressure at every wheel cylinder
pressure from the master cylinder reaches every wheel
reject: F2 equals F1 into A2 by A1

steps.memory_tip: One master cylinder, one pressure, four wheels — all braked together at the same instant.

insider_note: The lift and the brakes use the same law two different ways: the lift multiplies a force between two pistons, the brakes copy one pressure to four wheels at once.
